Notes: Event-study estimates of the relationship between firms’ energy intensity and own-price growth around each energy-price shock. Error bars show 90% confidence intervals. Source: Bank staff calculations. Latest observation: June 2026

Policy
To conclude, the recent surge in gas and oil prices has clearly increased near-term inflation risks and could push headline inflation considerably higher over the winter. But the key policy question is not the current level of energy prices alone. It is whether those prices remain elevated for long enough, and become broad enough, to generate more persistent inflationary pressure.
On the evidence so far, higher energy costs still appear largely concentrated within the energy complex itself rather than spreading widely through the economy. Monetary policy should respond to the risk that a relative-price shock becomes a general inflation process, not mechanically to every movement in the relative price itself. This is about judgements on propagation, not about denying the shock.
Evidence for significant second-round effects remains scant at present. Inflation in many energy-intensive goods and services categories has not accelerated as one might have expected after such a visible energy shock; food inflation has in fact fallen markedly and unexpectedly, though could rebound; and survey and producer-price indicators point to only modest pass-through so far. The labour market tells a similar story. Underlying wage growth appears broadly consistent with inflation returning to target over the medium term, and there is little sign of an emerging wage-price spiral.
Taken together, these developments suggest that the economy is proving less susceptible, at least so far, to a repeat of the inflation dynamics seen in 2022.
Nevertheless, there remains a nontrivial risk. Where views may differ on the Committee is on the extent to which we lean against these risks. Now, by holding Bank Rate fixed while financial conditions have tightened, policy has already become materially more restrictive relative to the outlook, and especially compared to the pre-war configuration in February. My view is that the current stance is also sufficiently restrictive, given the initial conditions of the economy in which the shock is hitting.
Against that backdrop, the case for further rate increases is not compelling to me unless energy prices remain high for an extended period and also generate clearer signals of a transmission into broader inflation persistence, as revealed by the signposts that we are actively monitoring.
The central judgement, then, must be whether the current energy shock remains a relative-price shock or evolves into a more general inflation process. That judgement has to combine both sides of the framework: the magnitude, duration and salience of the shock, and the initial conditions that determine whether it transmits. The available evidence currently points more toward the former interpretation.
That does not remove the need to stay alert. However, it does suggest, to me, that the burden of proof for additional tightening should rest on evidence that second-round effects are actually gaining traction, rather than on the existence of the energy shock alone.
That judgement, as ever, is conditional: if pressure builds and second-round effects begin to gain traction, the policy assessment would have to change. But symmetrically, if the economy evolves broadly as expected, with demand weakening and underlying domestic inflationary pressures continuing to moderate, then at some point, once energy risks abate, policy will need to move in the other direction — not because the risk has disappeared, but because maintaining an unnecessarily restrictive stance would itself carry costs.
The right policy response is therefore vigilant but disciplined. We should not deny the shock, nor dismiss the risk that it could propagate. But neither should monetary policy react mechanically to movements in energy prices if those movements remain primarily relative-price shocks.
The views expressed in this speech are not necessarily those of the Bank of England or the Monetary Policy Committee.

}The Light-1 CubeSat, used for scientific research. (Courtesy of NASA)Q&AEmissaryThe U.S. Has Weapons in Space. Now What?The acknowledgment has sparked fears of a new arms race with China and Russia.Link CopiedBy Chris O’Meara Published on Oct 1, 2026Why is the United States’ announcement of weapons in space noteworthy? Having operational weapons in space is not necessarily new or surprising. For decades, major powers such as the United States, China, and Russia have been developing and testing anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons, including systems that can be placed in orbit. However, what is new is that the statement constitutes the first public acknowledgment that the United States has a specifically designed space weapon stationed in orbit.In his announcement last month, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink provided some limited transparency regarding the increasingly militarized nature of outer space and the prospect of an arms race there. “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said. Space is generally recognized as a warfighting domain, and states developing ASAT technologies that can degrade, disrupt, or destroy their adversaries’ satellites is, for good or ill, a fact of operating within that domain. The weaponization of space remains a pressing concern for states and for international organizations like the United Nations.Why now?The principal rationale appears to be deterrence signaling, especially to the United States’ main adversaries in space, China and Russia, which have each developed ASAT weapons programs. The announcement might, therefore, be viewed as a calibrated response to U.S. rivals’ behavior, one that simply recognizes that all three states have been developing ASAT technologies, including those that can be placed in orbit, for a long time. In addition to deterrence, some limited transparency offered by the U.S. disclosure might be regarded as bringing stability to an increasingly contested domain. Some worry, however, that the announcement instead turns up the heat in orbit, with the weaponization of space becoming increasingly normalized, and prompts China and Russia to augment their existing capabilities to counter undisclosed U.S. technologies. Other states might also follow suit by developing and deploying their own space-based weapons, which increases the risks of proliferation and contestation in space to the detriment of both states and private commercial actors that operate there.What type of weapons are we talking about? States tend to keep these cards close to their chests, and Meink did not provide details of the nature, number, and placement of the weapons in orbit.However, he did speak of “space control weapons,” which refers to the U.S. policy of seeking to achieve and maintain “space superiority,” including through the use of ASAT technologies, which are typically grouped into four broad categories:Kinetic physical ASAT weapons, such as anti-satellite missiles or other methods of physical kinetic attacks directed against satellites (such as projectiles, robotic arms that can grab satellites, and chemical sprayers)Non-kinetic physical ASAT weapons, including lasers and high-powered microwavesElectronic ASAT weapons, such as jamming devices that interfere with the transmission of signals to and from satellites and spoofing devices that can falsify such signalsCyberattacks against space systemsDepending on the technology, the weapon might be launched from Earth (including land, sea, and air platforms) or from orbit, and it might also be used against land-based space infrastructure, such as satellite ground stations.Experts have speculated that the “space control weapons” referred to by Meink are orbital weapons and likely to be electronic warfare or radio jamming platforms, rather than the kinetic and more destructive type of weapon, although the latter cannot be ruled out.How have U.S. adversaries responded?Negatively. China cautioned against an arms race in outer space, and Russia asserted that space must be free of any weapons. Russia also reiterated the call for a “legally binding instrument” that would prevent the use of force against space objects. The United States has previously been critical of Chinese and Russian proposals for a dedicated treaty banning the placement and use of weapons in space due to a lack of effective means to verify compliance with any treaty.With these responses, China and Russia are ostensibly setting themselves against war in space. Yet a recent U.S. assessment shows that both states continue to develop their own ASAT weapons, with the threat growing in scale, complexity, and aggressiveness. Space experts agree that China and Russia are developing a range of ASAT capabilities, in addition to other states like Iran, North Korea, India, Israel, and some European states, to varying and lesser degrees. The greatest fear relates to Russia, which might be developing a nuclear space-based weapon as part of its arsenal. This would be a uniquely dangerous threat to us all. Accordingly, the space environment is increasingly unstable, and this is before other emerging technologies, such as autonomous space systems powered by AI, are added into the mix.What have U.S. allies said?Very little publicly, with the exception of the UK. Following the U.S. announcement, the UK likewise confirmed that it is “developing capabilities for orbital warfare.” The UK also announced the creation of a Royal Air Force squadron dedicated to defending UK satellites from hostile threats. In 2023, France publicly declared its intention to build and launch a satellite equipped with a high-powered laser, so signaling the importance of space and of protecting space assets seems to be a recent theme. It will be worth watching whether other allies now follow suit.Is it legal under international law for the United States to deploy ASAT weapons in space?The United States is unlikely to have breached existing international law simply by deploying a space-based weapon. However, the legality of its conduct would ultimately depend on how that weapon is used.Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which is the main space law treaty, explicitly bans placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, installing them on celestial bodies, or otherwise stationing such weapons in outer space. The moon and other celestial bodies are also fully demilitarized by Article IV and may only be used for peaceful purposes. However, international law does not prohibit other types of weapons, including conventional ASAT weapons placed in orbit. States may use these technologies for lawful purposes, such as necessary and proportionate acts of self-defense conducted in accordance with international humanitarian law.Specific international legal regulation of ASAT weapons is currently lacking, although there are laudable ongoing multilateral efforts to prevent an arms race in outer space. The UN General Assembly has called for all states to commit to not conducting destructive ASAT missile tests, and several states, including the United States, have unilaterally agreed to this. However, a multilateral ban on placing and using ASAT weapons is unlikely in the current geopolitical climate.Without a multilateral ban, how can ASAT weapon use be limited?The focus of my recent and ongoing research has been to think about how existing international law applies to ASAT weapon use, even when states use these weapons in self-defense (which Meink appeared to contemplate). My argument is that, without a multilateral ASAT weapons control treaty, there are bodies of international law, not originally conceived of as applying beyond the Earth’s atmosphere, that can be interpreted and applied to space. These bodies of law include (but are not limited to) international law governing the use of force (anchored in the UN Charter) and international humanitarian law, which both set limits regarding when and how states may lawfully target satellites using ASAT technologies, including in self-defense. Although the current U.S. administration is dismissive of international law, states generally accept that it applies in space. The United States, NATO, and EU allies have previously expressed their commitment to responsible behavior in space and to acting in space in accordance with international law. Given the unique nature of the space environment and the importance of satellites to modern societies, compliance with these rules means that ASAT weapon use of all kinds—even in defensive military operations—would be heavily restricted and may even be prohibited in all but the most extreme circumstances of self-defense. Just because you deploy a weapon in space does not mean that you get to use it freely, without considering the ramifications.Why is limiting ASAT use so important?Tactically, targeting an adversary’s satellites with ASAT weapons could offer a state a significant military advantage in conflict. Modern militaries rely heavily on satellite-provided services to conduct warfare, so neutralizing your adversary’s satellites reflects the idea that whoever wins in space also wins on Earth.Yet the ramifications of ASAT weapon use for states, corporations, and individuals could be disastrous. Potential space debris resulting from ASAT weapon use (especially of the kinetic kind) can be incredibly long-lasting and threatens all other satellites in orbit. Many of these satellites underpin the operation of global societies and economies. Take U.S. GPS and its equivalents. Although many may think of this technology’s role in mapping apps and fitness trackers, GPS is central to running many essential services, including agriculture, aviation, banking systems, power grids, emergency services, and more. Conflict in space leading to even a temporary GPS disruption could therefore have catastrophic effects on civilians and state interests, both on Earth and in space.This is why space debris caused by ASAT weapon use has been emphasized by the United States itself as a major concern, including in response to the controversial Russian ASAT missile test in 2021. As space becomes increasingly congested with ever more satellites being launched by states and private actors, the potentially catastrophic risk posed by ASAT weapon use multiplies. We must avoid making space unusable.How does the law address these risks?The law allows states to effectively defend themselves, but within guardrails that require states to account for the consequences that flow from targeting an adversary’s satellite during conflict.Non-kinetic methods such as jamming, laser dazzling, spoofing, and limited cyber operations against satellite systems must be preferred to using destructive kinetic ASAT weapons. The latter type of weapons should generally be regarded as off the table to avoid the risk of space debris and civilian harm. Earth-based targets, such as satellite control centers, should also be preferred over targeting satellites with any form of ASAT weapon. Indeed, as recent events show, targeting supporting terrestrial infrastructure might be just as effective as directly targeting the satellites themselves and avoids the risks of conducting warfare in space. The imperative to protect space and space-provided services from the effects of military activities in this way benefits us all, including the strategic interests of the United States. My argument is that compliance with the existing law reflects and protects this essential need.What will you be watching for as this story evolves?Other states’ responses will be interesting to note, especially if the U.S. announcement encourages other states to follow suit because it is viewed as a further legitimization of space-based weapons. The next meeting of the UN working group on this topic is scheduled for November, and I am keen to see if this and other multilateral arms control efforts can make progress and keep pace with the rapid technological developments that we are witnessing.I will also be watching to see if the push for restraint filters beyond typical expert groups and brings further transparency to state actions. Perhaps the announcement by Meink can shine a light on the existence and capabilities of these weapons and the potentially catastrophic dangers that they pose to our everyday lives here on Earth. I hope this renewed focus will spur the development of meaningful regulation and (re)commitments by states to responsible behavior in space.Get more news and analysis fromEmissaryThe latest from Carnegie scholars on the world’s most pressing challenges, delivered to your inbox.About the AuthorChris O’Meara British Academy Global Innovation Fellow, Global Order and Institutions ProgramChris O’Meara is a British Academy Global Innovation Fellow in the Global Order and Institutions Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.Arms ControlTechnologyForeign PolicyGlobal GovernanceUnited StatesRussiaChinaCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from EmissaryCommentaryEmissaryWho Gets to Put Guardrails on AI?Why governance of rapidly evolving technology will be distributed and complex.Stewart Patrick, Scott SingerCommentaryEmissaryThe UN Isn’t Declining. It’s Decomposing.Washington’s decision to support some UN functions while letting others wither is pulling the organization apart at the seams.Stewart Patrick, Theodore ZaritskyCommentaryEmissaryWhat’s Driving the Trump Administration’s Push to Dismantle the ICC?The move is an escalation of its war on multilateralism.Stewart PatrickCommentaryEmissaryCarney’s Remarkable Message to Middle PowersAnd how they can respond.+1Sophia Besch, Steve Feldstein, Stewart Patrick, …CommentaryEmissaryThe G20 Agenda Is Shifting from the Global South to America FirstFor four years, the G20’s emerging economies used the rotating presidency to set an unprecedented agenda. With the United States now at the helm, that’s about to dramatically change.Gustavo Romero, Stewart Patrick

articles.title: Market update - October 2nd 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Market update - October 2nd, 20262 min readDataHike odds fell, long yields hit a 24-year high, and Bitcoin consolidated Bitcoin has benefited this week from a sharp reduction in near-term rate hike expectations. The catalyst was initially New York Fed President John Williams, who argued that September’s 25bp hike had reduced the urgency for further tightening and that the Fed now had time to assess incoming data. Markets responded quickly, with the implied probability of an October hike falling from roughly 75% to around 50%. Subsequent data have pushed expectations lower still, with markets now assigning roughly a 37% probability of an October hike.The economic data itself has become more mixed. August JOLTS openings fell to 7.079M, below expectations and the lowest in five months, while September consumer confidence dropped sharply to 81.9 from 88.6, its weakest level since 2014. Both point toward softer labour demand and increasing pressure on the consumer. The latest PCE data were also relatively encouraging: core inflation rose 0.2% month-on-month and 3.0% year-on-year, below expectations, helping reinforce the argument for patience from the Fed.The front end repriced, the direction did not The picture is far from uniformly weak, however. Second-quarter GDP was revised to 2.2% annualised, consumer spending rose a strong 0.9% in August and initial jobless claims have fallen to their lowest since July. The Fed is therefore looking at an unusual combination of softer forward-looking employment and sentiment indicators alongside relatively resilient underlying activity.For Bitcoin, the reduction in rate expectations has been supportive. It reinforces just how sensitive the asset remains to monetary policy and dollar liquidity in the short term. Lower expected policy rates reduce the relative attractiveness of cash and short-duration Treasuries and typically improve the backdrop for Bitcoin and other liquidity-sensitive assets.What is unusual is the behaviour of the Treasury market. While futures have materially reduced expectations for an October hike, longer-dated yields have continued moving higher. The 10-year Treasury briefly reached around 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. This divergence suggests investors are increasingly distinguishing between Fed policy at the front end of the curve and concerns around fiscal sustainability, heavy Treasury issuance and term premium at the long end.That is potentially important for Bitcoin. Falling policy-rate expectations are supportive through the conventional liquidity channel, while rising long-term yields increasingly reflect concern about US fiscal sustainability rather than simply tighter monetary policy. If that distinction becomes more pronounced, Bitcoin could benefit from both a softer expected Fed path and renewed demand for non-sovereign assets.Fund flows, however, show that investors remain cautious. We have seen only around US$150M of inflows so far this week, a dramatic slowdown from approximately US$3.5B last week. The change does not yet look like a reversal in sentiment, but it does suggest that investors are becoming more selective after such a strong period of inflows.Overall, the macro backdrop has improved for Bitcoin, but it remains finely balanced. Softer employment, confidence and inflation data have reduced the need for another immediate hike, while the persistence of very high long-term Treasury yields is creating a separate fiscal concern. Both developments could ultimately prove supportive for Bitcoin, albeit through very different channels.Published onOct 2nd, 2026WriterJames ButterfillHead of ResearchFormer Head of Research at ETF Securities, James leads CoinShares' Research department with deep expertise in equity and fund management.

articles.title: Daily: US equities can gain further after record highs
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Why higher rates and greater dispersion can benefit hedge funds (5 mins)Video: Market Playbook | The investment case for consumer agents (5 mins)Podcast: Signal over Noise | The 1999 analogue through a fixed income lens, on Apple , SpotifyThought of the dayThe S&P 500 rose 0.6% on Tuesday to its first record high since August, bringing its year-to-date gain to 14.2%. The all-time peak came despite the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and US Treasury yields remaining at multi-decade highs.But while periods of volatility are likely, we think the rally will keep going. Recent developments underscore our view that further gains should be supported by AI investment, strong corporate earnings, and solid economic growth.Strong AI demand and investment remain a key driving force. Renewed strength in the AI trade has supported the latest rally, with encouraging adoption from recent model and product launches adding to investor confidence. Without taking any single-stock views, Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast to above Wall Street estimates and provided an upbeat long-term earnings outlook amid growing demand for custom data center chips and other AI hardware. This points to continued demand for AI compute and infrastructure overall, which should underpin further investments. We expect global AI-related capex to grow over 33% to USD 1.2tr in 2027, providing a powerful earnings tailwind for part of the AI ecosystem. Consensus estimates project the Nasdaq 100 to grow earnings by 43% this year and 28% next year.Earnings growth is broadening beyond tech. While the recent rally was driven by tech, the earnings story is broader than AI. We estimate earnings growth of 25% for the S&P 500 this year, followed by another 14% increase in 2027. The tech sector should remain a major contributor, but we also expect profits to rise across other industries. Resilient consumer spending should support consumer discretionary, robust capital market activity and a recovery in loan growth should benefit financials, and cyclical manufacturing improvement should lead to solid growth in industrials. We also like health care and utilities for their defensive characteristics and exposure to structural growth opportunities.Resilient economic growth should help equities absorb higher rates. The US trade deficit widened in August to its largest since March 2025, which could present a near-term drag on headline growth. But robust imports reflect firm consumer demand and investment in equipment, including AI-related capital spending. We forecast US GDP growth of 2.2% this year and 2% in 2027, providing a favorable backdrop for companies to grow and generate profits. This resilience should also help the economy withstand modest policy tightening from the Federal Reserve. Across the 16 hiking cycles since 1954, the S&P 500 gained an average of 10.8% in the year following the first Fed hike. With current economic conditions consistent with continued expansion, we believe earnings growth can offset some of the valuation pressure from higher interest rates.So, investors should remain positioned for market upside, and we forecast the S&P 500 to reach 8,400 by June next year. We stress the importance of broadly diversified exposure across sectors and regions. Investors can also consider capital preservation strategies for more defensive positioning.

articles.title: 3 Client Acquisition Tips for Wealth Management Firms | BNY
articles.text:
First Niche, Then Pitch: 3 Ways to Target and Win the Clients You Want

Specialization doesn’t shrink your market — it’s how you grow faster and command higher margins.

alarm

6 minute read

calendar_today

06 Oct, 2026

Introduction

Failure to define a niche can result in wasted marketing resources and a lack of growth. Determining who you want to target, why and how — with clearly defined targets and metrics — will enable more consistent growth.
While a rigorous market analysis and developed strategy are critical, a Broadridge study found that only 23% of advisors have a documented marketing plan. Advisors with a clear plan convert digital leads 168% more often than those who do not, adding 50% more clients each year. This suggests that many firms execute marketing tactics without a clear strategy, making it difficult to measure impact or ROI.
We recently spoke with senior executives from several wealth management firms to discuss how focus, metrics and scalability can help marketing drive greater business growth. This conversation resulted in three clear ways to target and win the right clients.

Define Your Niche Based on the Right Criteria

Your niche is the foundation of your marketing strategy. Know which clients you are trying to serve — not based on revenue or assets, but on the specific problems your firm solves best and most frequently. Without a clear niche, your channel spend will not drive the growth you want.
The belief that specialization shrinks a firm’s addressable market is wrong. One CEO noted that her firm grew AUM from $500 million to $5 billion and doubled margins by focusing on niches. When you’re positioned as the clear expert for a certain segment, you stop competing on price and start winning on it. Digital reach has made physical proximity to clients less critical; when your firm’s positioning is clear and specific, the right prospects self-select.
Quick take on spotting a niche: Take your full client base; strip out revenue and assets as qualifiers; run them through 5 to 10 behavioral and problem-focused criteria; then market to that client archetype. Ask your best clients if they know someone who shares their characteristics and challenges. Client referrals represent the highest-ROI, zero-cost starting point for your niche approach.

Market to Your Niche — With the Right Measurements

Don’t spend money on marketing — not even directionally — if you can’t measure results. The right KPIs are not volume metrics, but rather cost per lead, lead-to-close rate and customer acquisition cost. Consider client lifetime value: $10,000 may seem steep to acquire a single client, but not against a potential 10-year relationship generating recurring fees.
You cannot measure what you cannot control. Develop a repeatable niche marketing process with fixed touchpoints in a consistent sequence or the data you collect will be unreliable. Standardization is the underpinning of all marketing ROI analysis.
Wealth management traditionally defined personalization as investment customization and high-touch service. But today’s clients want to feel understood personally. They judge you by the experience you deliver — through your discovery process, resources, team and tailored services.
Partner events can be a growth lever in a niche strategy. Expand your view beyond estate planners and accountants, and include other professionals who help to solve the problems of your niche market. Think about employment attorneys for executive women, branding experts for executives building their professional identity or concierge doctors for clients focused on longevity. Help your clients manage life, not just money — and they will value these personal services.

Personalize Your Niche to Drive Growth

To grow in your niche, you need to know what to standardize and what to customize. Identify the aspects of your service model that can be systematized and what requires personalization. Take advantage of opportunities to scale when developing tactics. For example, build content you can use across stakeholder relationships, such as short educational podcasts that can be shared with both clients and advisors.
Integrate AI prudently. The human factor is what will win and keep your niche clients. Our executive panelists agreed that AI-generated personas and training tools are valuable starting points for discovery and advisor development. But the remaining value — lived experience, listening, the ability to read the client — remains human.
Growth isn’t merely about doing more, but rather developing a structure that allows advisors to be fully present where and when it matters most to the client.

Building Lasting Value

To deliver its maximum value, marketing must continually build enterprise value, not just increase success for a few rainmakers. Firms preparing for succession or M&A need a marketing engine that drives growth for every advisor. This is what distinguishes a firm with a premium valuation from one dependent on a few key people.
Firms that will win in the years ahead will be intentional, not exhaustive, in their marketing approach. Grounded in carefully chosen market niches, they will execute a strategy based on who they serve, how they build trust and where human engagement creates the greatest value.

articles.title: Canada's carbon pricing at a crossroads | RBCCM
articles.text:
Last week, in partnership with ClearBlue Markets, we had the privilege of hosting an exclusive, off-the-record roundtable during the Energy Disruptors Summit in Calgary, Alberta. We brought together 15 senior voices from across Oil and Gas, Power and Utilities, and Industry for a candid conversation on the state of industrial carbon pricing in Canada. Key themes emerged amidst this period of generational change for carbon and economic policy in Canada, along with a notion that there is an opportunity for a win-win for both climate and economic growth if we manage to get this right.

Here are our top takeaways:
1. Policy certainty is the single most important input but remains elusive
If there was one theme that united participants across every sector, it was this: without long-term, credible policy certainty, nothing else in the carbon market ecosystem can function as intended. Investors cannot allocate capital, project developers cannot secure financing, and banks cannot provide liquidity. One participant made a particularly striking observation, that even if a program like the Clean Fuel Regulations technically ran through to 2050, but did so on a year-to-year basis without a firm federal commitment, the market would still be uninvestable, even if the program outperformed all expectations. This highlights how the signal for the market matters just as much as the substance of the market itself.
A necessary part of this is the federal government being unequivocal about the purpose of industrial carbon pricing. In the absence of any other meaningful climate policy instrument in Canada, carbon pricing is effectively the only mechanism capable of driving emissions reductions. Saying that clearly and consistently would go a long way.
2. Financial infrastructure is a must
Quebec’s linkage to the Western Climate Initiative was broadly described as a success story from a market perspective. The WCI’s mature financial ecosystem, deep liquidity, sophisticated hedging instruments, robust price discovery, and an options market that helps smooth volatility, is what separates a functional carbon market from one that stays in its infancy. The contrast is stark, participants noted that you can relatively easily offload $1 billion of risk for up to five years in the WCI but cannot execute a $1 million, two-year hedge in Ontario. No other Canadian carbon market currently has this infrastructure and that gap will continue to hamper any ambition to scale. The good news is that financial sophistication follows certainty so if you can build the policy foundation, then the market infrastructure will come.
3. The price debate is less about the headline number and more about the collar
There was healthy debate on the carbon price trajectory, with some arguing the near-term priority should be establishing the floor price as described in the Canada-Alberta MOU, and others noting that several provincial programs, BC’s in particular, remain closely indexed to the headline number. What the group broadly agreed on is that the WCI’s price collar model, a defined floor and ceiling with price containments / market stability reserves, is the right design for managing volatility, supporting investment certainty, and enabling long-term project financing. The collar gives both supply and demand participants what they actually need, a range they can plan around.
4. Focus on the carrot or the stick?
Several participants raised whether Canada is at risk of over-indexing on carbon market mechanisms at the expense of direct investment incentives, such as investment tax credits, production tax credits or providing additional value for lower carbon commodities (ex. lower carbon oil or steel). The concern is not that carbon pricing is wrong, but that it is working in a vacuum. Without complementary incentives for low-carbon products, the carbon price creates a compliance cost without fully creating an investment case. The most durable frameworks are likely to be those that combine both.
5. The CFR is becoming a successful Pan-Canadian carbon market, but challenges to growth remain
Participants broadly viewed the Clean Fuel Regulations as a credible national carbon market in its early stages — but its primary spot market structure and short track record make it difficult to finance against. The ask from industry is straightforward: make it a binding, long-term commitment and more importantly, reframe it. A carbon program tied explicitly to industrial policy, i.e. jobs, economic growth, and attracting foreign direct investment, has political durability in a way that a standalone climate instrument simply does not. The lesson from other jurisdictions is that the markets that have scaled are the ones that solved for both.
6. ITMOs offer a dual-sided opportunity for Canada
The federal government’s exploration of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) generated optimism in the room. On the supply side, Canadian companies — particularly in engineered carbon removals — are well-positioned to generate and sell high-quality credits to foreign governments. On the demand side, allowing heavy emitters to purchase ITMOs to offset emissions growth tied to economic expansion could meaningfully benefit the broader economy while preserving compliance integrity. It is one of the more compelling near-term levers available to policymakers.
7. A Pan-Canadian carbon market — or something bolder — is the long-term answer
The fragmentation of Canada’s carbon market landscape was a recurring source of frustration. A Pan-Canadian market would directly resolve the liquidity gaps and financial complexity that currently limit scalability, and participants broadly agreed the logic is compelling. But the most provocative idea of the session came from one participant who went further: why not explore Canada joining the EU Emissions Trading System as part of its associate membership in the EU? The group acknowledged that this would, in theory, resolve most of the existing market challenges in one move — delivering the depth, liquidity, and financial infrastructure that no Canadian market currently has. However, it was recognised as likely impractical given the makeup of Canada’s economy versus the EU’s, among other challenges. Regardless, any form of a Pan-Canadian market will require bold vision, political will and compromise from all the provinces and territories, but the opportunity to make this work is too large to ignore.
RBC’s capabilities
To help navigate the rapidly evolving carbon markets, RBC Capital Markets offers extensive expertise and full capabilities in emissions trading across both compliance and voluntary carbon markets. The Environmental Markets Solutions Group partners with RBC Capital Markets’ Environmental Commodities desk, established in 2008, to offer bespoke solutions to clients looking to operationalize their net-zero targets through carbon and renewable energy solutions.
In April 2023, RBC announced a strategic investment and partnership with ClearBlue Markets, an award-winning carbon markets advisory firm. ClearBlue Markets provides carbon markets services to hundreds of clients worldwide, helping them optimize their strategies for compliance requirements and voluntary net zero ambitions through its deep advisory expertise and AI enabled technology.

Corporate Law and Transformation

Group reorganizations and transformations come in many forms, domestic or cross-border, transaction-driven or strategic. EY Corporate Law and Transformation teams help businesses design and provide legally robust, commercially efficient structures, combining corporate law knowledge with multidisciplinary delivery to achieve value-added and integrated transformation outcomes.

The team

Craig Stevenson

EY Global Corporate Law and Transformation Leader

What EY can do for you
Corporate transformations and reorganizations can present huge opportunities for groups with common objectives, including the need for an optimal pre-deal transaction perimeter, a value-additive post-deal integration, a tax-informed reorganization, an operating model redesign to align with a new business strategy, group-wide legal entity rationalizations to cut cost, simplify structures and improve governance and so on.
Some of the triggers for transformation can involve:
Complex and fragmented group structures that are difficult to manage and tough to align with business strategyTransaction-driven change requiring pre-deal business separation or post-deal integration, often involving mixed business units in cross-border structures and tight timelinesEvolving regulatory, legal and tax expectations across multiple jurisdictions driving changes to group structuresInefficient group structures with redundant or duplicative entities, often the legacy of deal activityThe need to simplify operating and legal entity models ahead of significant events such as ERP implementation or new go-to-market strategies
EY Corporate Law and Transformation teams routinely help organizations navigate this often-complex environment by providing comprehensive, integrated support across the overall transformation lifecycle. EY professionals and teams provide corporate law offerings alongside tax, accounting and other capabilities under one coordinated approach, across the world. Input into feasibility assessments, design of the target structure, and full drafting and implementation supportLocal law support delivered by one of the largest global legal networksExperienced project management teams who routinely lead and coordinate some of the most complex, highest-value reorganizations for some of the largest groups in the worldClose collaboration with other EY teams helping identify and resolve issues early and efficiently, lowering project risk and adding valueRobust execution of complex transformations by corporate lawyers who routinely undertake such projects, supported by consistent, coordinated delivery across countries and with deliverables and advice aligned with your other EY engagement teams
Why EY
Our Corporate Law and Transformation lawyers regularly advise on complex, high-value, multinational carve-out transactions and are consistently recognized by leading legal directories, with many practitioners receiving individual market accolades. articles.title: Energy prices surged in September; non-energy prices edged up—Pink Sheet
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Energy prices surged in September; non-energy prices edged up—Pink Sheet

Maria Hazel Macadangdang

John Baffes

October 06, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The energy price index surged by 25.7% in September, led by crude oil (+21.2%) and natural gas (+15.3%), according to the World Bank's Pink Sheet. The non-energy index edged up by 1.3%.
Agricultural prices rose 1.6% in September, with food gaining 3.8% and raw materials edging up 0.9%, while beverages prices fell 4.6%. Fertilizer prices changed little at 0.4%.
Metals rose almost 1%in September, with zinc up 3.8%, partly offset by tin declining 3.0%. Precious metals eased 1.9%, with gold falling 2.1% and silver 1.2%.
The Pink Sheet is a monthly report that monitors commodity price movements.

Maria Hazel Macadangdang

Research Analyst, Prospects Group, World Bank

articles.text:
Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Most recent

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing

Great Tech In Search Of Profits

AJ Cortese, Laila Khawaja
5 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies held its inaugural China Tech Tour with 19 institutional-investor clients. Through a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives, we examined China’s semiconductor, AI, new energy, robotics and biotechnology industries. This week’s China Tech Brief explores some of the key findings. By far the biggest theme was the gap between technological capabilities and corporate returns. China has plenty of globally competitive tech companies, but few that generate really attractive earnings.

Gavekal Technologies: Chips

GavekalTech On The Ground: 2026 China Tech Trip Takeaways

Laila Khawaja
1 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies made its inaugural China Tech Trip with 19 institutional investor clients. The trip offered a close-up view of China’s tech ecosystem, including semiconductors, AI, new energy, robotics, and biotech, via a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives. This week’s Chips report summarizes our observations in the semiconductor and AI sectors.

More research

Chinese EV Makers’ European Offensive

28 Sep 2026

Chinese EV makers have conquered their home market and are on track to export over 5mn vehicles this year, double the 2025 figure. Their next move will be to start moving production offshore, to get closer to key markets and evade tariffs. The biggest target is Europe, where half a dozen projects are under way and many more are planned.

Webinar: The State Of China Tech

25 Sep 2026

As presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare for their summit meeting in Washington, China’s fast-growing technology capabilities are a major topic. The big questions at the moment are how close Chinese artificial-intelligence labs are to matching the US frontier models, and whether the two sides can start negotiating rules on AI safety. But behind those lie even bigger questions: What is the balance of technological power between the US and China? And how far can the world's two big tech powers go in pulling apart the thick webs of interdependence that tie them together?

Breaking Up Is Hard To Do

21 Sep 2026

Both China and the US have devoted intense energy to slashing their technological reliance on each other. These efforts have had some impact, but the overall lesson is that decoupling is really difficult and even as old dependencies are cut, new ones pop up. This China Tech Brief examines the underlying causes.

The China New Energy Guidebook

16 Sep 2026

Over the past year Gavekal Technologies has explored most corners of China’s vast and unique energy system, with a particular focus on how electrification is transforming China’s economy and its position in the world. We have now distilled our insights into our first annual China New Energy Guidebook. This concise presentation outlines China’s strategies for its energy and electricity systems, assesses the progress of wind, solar and nuclear deployment, and analyzes the key electricity related sectors: batteries, electric vehicles, AI and the “electrotech stack.”

A China Tech Report Card

9 Sep 2026

Over the past year Gavekal Technologies has tracked China’s progress across a range of tech sectors. Today we take a step back and try to assess its overall capabilities. First, outside a handful of areas, China is still more of a fast follower than a global pace-setter. Second, China’s well-documented manufacturing dominance is mainly in products of medium or low complexity. Finally, China’s tech ecosystem still relies heavily on foreign-sourced components, equipment and intellectual property.

The Deployment Challenge For Cheap Solar

31 Aug 2026

For most of the past two decades, the solar story was about making the panel cheaper. China has solved that problem. Thanks to massive excess capacity, Chinese producers are not making much money. With equipment now a commodity, the economic value of solar will mainly come from its installation. The broadest local benefits are likely to come in countries that can figure out how to scale up distributed solar generation at homes and businesses.

articles.title: Consumer Checkpoint: Strength in numbers
articles.text: David Tinsley Joe Wadford Liz Everett Krisberg Taylor Bowley Vanessa Cook Lynelle Huskey October 2026 Consumer spending remained very solid in September. Bank of America aggregated credit and debit card spending per household rose 6.2% year-over-year (YoY), or 5.1% excluding gasoline, both the third strongest growth rates over the past four years. Month-over-month (MoM) spending was more muted, especially without gas. Spending shows considerable breadth: the vast majority of discretionary retail and services categories are showing growth. Moreover, this strength extends across income cohorts, with the ongoing recovery of lower- and middle-income households' spending growth. With the winter months fast approaching, holiday spending is already increasing at a solid rate, though it's still early. In Bank of America deposit data through September, buy now, pay later (BNPL) usage is rising but not at a rate that is overly concerning. However, nearly one in every five households that use BNPL has a repayment of over $500. Read our full analysis for a more in-depth look at these trends. Consumer Checkpoint is a regular publication from Bank of America Institute. It aims to provide a holistic and real-time estimate of U.S. consumers’ spending and their financial well-being, leveraging the depth and breadth of Bank of America proprietary data. Any such Bank of America proprietary data is not intended to be reflective or indicative of, and should not be relied upon as, the results of operations, financial conditions or performance of Bank of America. articles.title: Who gets Venezuela's next barrel?
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Who gets Venezuela's next barrel?

Anna Gelpern (PIIE),

Katherine Shen (Georgetown Law) and

Marcelo Marzouka (Georgetown Law)

Date
October 2, 2026 4:13 PM

Photo Credit: REUTERS/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria

The authors are grateful to Adnan Mazarei, Alejandro Werner, and Ángel Ubide for comments on an earlier version of this post.

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Until recently, the subject of claim priorities in sovereign debt restructuring was mostly confined to academic journals.(link is external) For better or worse, creditors had acted as if they were equal—or pari passu.(link is external) No more. Venezuela's creditors are poised for a global asset "grab race"(link is external) that could make its debt restructuring not only the biggest but also the messiest in history. The defining question is their place in queue: Who gets the marginal dollar from each additional barrel of recovering oil production? Legacy bondholders? Arbitration decision winners? Banks, bilateral lenders, new investors? Or the Venezuelan public?
The answer is anyone's guess. It depends on the claim terms, the creditors who hold them, and the tribunals resolving the inevitable disputes. Much of this information remains a mystery, with no obvious path into the light. Corporate restructurings offer a useful contrast: If an oil company filed for bankruptcy protection, a full map of its liabilities and the assets available to meet them would soon emerge under court supervision.
Sovereign debt has no mechanism for bringing all claims into the light and dealing with them in one consolidated proceeding. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), for all its flaws, has served as a central information hub and offered a semblance of a restructuring framework since the 1980s. Without it, cataloguing claims against Venezuela's government and its various agencies and parastatals is a tall order. Iraq's debt restructuring in 2003 is often cited as precedent, but the context was rather different. The IMF was involved,(link is external) and the UN Security Council and major financial jurisdictions shielded Iraq's oil revenues,(link is external) with an independent auditor to keep track of financial flows.(link is external) No such framework exists in Venezuela. The United States has sought to supply an alternative centralized mechanism;(link is external) Its elements are still emerging.
On the bright side, most of the information gaps in Venezuela's case belong to the category of known unknowns(link is external). Finding an orderly way to manage them can point the way forward for debtors, creditors, and the international community. Getting it wrong will have harmful consequences far beyond Venezuela.
Here is what we know we don't know.
The full list of claims and the creditors
Researchers for the #PublicDebtIsPublic(link is external) initiative have assembled the most comprehensive public record of the claims(link is external) against Venezuela from dozens of repositories, registries, and court dockets. These span arbitration awards, court judgments, bonds, bilateral and multilateral loans, and a jumble of guaranteed, collateralized, and quasi-collateralized arrangements. More than US$20 billion in International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) awards(link is external) remain outstanding, including US$8.7 billion for ConocoPhillips(link is external), the largest in ICSID history. Claims registered in Delaware alone exceed US$19 billion(link is external). Unsecured bondholders hold roughly US$60 billion(link is external) in face value, alongside roughly US$2 billion(link is external) in 2020 secured bonds issued by Venezuelan stated-owned oil company Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA)(link is external). China is owed at least US$18 billion(link is external), Russia US$4 billion(link is external), and multilateral lenders, led by the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF) and the Inter-American Development Bank, US$4 billion(link is external). Unpaid and penalty interest could yield a multiple of these numbers.
Creditors do not map neatly onto claims. Over Venezuela's decade in default and under sanctions(link is external), many have traded, syndicated, hedged, and secured their exposures. A ticket to the restructuring need not reflect the holder's economic interest in the outcome(link is external). Moreover, some creditors will not be at the table even as they hold enforceable claims: Some cannot participate, others may choose not to, and those with direct access to Venezuela's revenues may not need to.
Restructuring perimeters and priorities
Venezuela's restructuring perimeter has yet to be disclosed(link is external), but there is already talk of maneuvering around its edges(link is external). Some creditors that can get paid directly from export revenues could try to stay outside the restructuring perimeter, leaving those inside to subsidize their exit. Others could try to leverage uncertainty around international recognition to introduce frictions in the restructuring process, building on past legal challenges to Venezuelan government authority(link is external).
The IMF has warned(link is external), most recently a year ago, that sovereign debt with opaque collateral features undermined trust and inter-creditor equity, delayed crisis resolution, and put sustainable outcomes at risk. Venezuela risks becoming a case study. Its debt to one large state-owned bank is paid out of oil proceeds that flow directly into an account at the bank, with setoff rights(link is external). The state-owned oil giant PDVSA has meanwhile converted unpaid bills to service providers into notes(link is external) with ambiguous(link is external) seniority(link is external).
Creditors have always jockeyed for priority and kept an eye on the exits when a sovereign sinks into distress. A rickety old international coordination architecture kept such efforts to the margins but often failed to achieve durable debt relief. Now more creditors come armed with creative new tools to get paid first, with contract terms and legal rules behind them cloaked in secrecy.
The creativity signals that debtors and creditors are losing faith in legacy architecture and could propel a self-fulfilling prophecy. As hidden claims accumulate, restructuring legitimacy and finality get harder to attain.
Parallel tracks and layered deals
Venezuela launched its restructuring in May(link is external) without the IMF, relying on a stock estimate(link is external) and debt sustainability analysis that is yet to be published or independently verified.
Without the IMF's machinery or a credible substitute, bondholders negotiate on one track, bilateral lenders on another, investors on a third, with no central reference frame, not even one to argue against while the courts distribute assets and proceeds across jurisdictions.
At least in theory, a US executive order issued on January 9, 2026(link is external), supplies a centralizing framework of sorts: It shields the proceeds of Venezuela's natural resource exports from the US judicial process and limits pathways for debt enforcement. As sanction carveouts expand, more revenues may flow into special accounts established under the January 9 executive order(link is external), but tracking these transactions is a challenge(link is external). Meanwhile, the August 31 US-Venezuela oil agreement(link is external) layers a new set of transactions on an already complex and opaque debt stock. Most of the new fields in the agreement had been controlled by Russian and Chinese firms. Which tribunals might resolve the competing claims to oil and oil revenues, under what rules, and to what end, is another question for the not-so-distant future(link is external).
A test for international debt architecture?
Tracking the full list of claims against a sovereign is a challenge increasingly common in a sovereign debt ecosystem defined by extreme creditor diversity, resource competition, and a fraying coordination architecture. Hidden debt scandals have become a regular feature of sovereign restructuring, but opacity does not arrive with restructuring. It starts with public debt disclosure practice long before loans are made and side deals are struck. By the time creditors reach the restructuring table, forensic accounting and priority contests cause delays and deadweight losses that harm everyone—here, none more than the Venezuelan citizens, who bear the costs of untangling murky deals signed in their name.
Transparency is a rare point of multilateral consensus. The G7(link is external) and the G20(link is external) have endorsed debt transparency in communiques for more than a decade. Venezuela shows why acting on this consensus is essential—and urgent.
Robust transparency is indispensable when resources cannot grow without large-scale investment, the claim queue keeps lengthening, and trust is in short supply. More information seeps into the public domain day by day. A durable settlement in Venezuela will need to have broad-based buy-in and rest on published, verifiable data on the claims against it, the claim terms, the creditors who hold them, and the resources available to meet them. Getting it right in Venezuela could give international debt architecture reform a fighting chance.

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.
