articles.title: Sri Lanka’s Economic and Geopolitical Balancing Act
articles.text: Source: GettyArticleSri Lanka’s Economic and Geopolitical Balancing ActEconomic recovery has brought Sri Lanka a modicum of stability, but domestic strains and great-power rivalry could test how long it lasts.Link CopiedBy Avinash PaliwalPublished on Oct 6, 2026IntroductionOn March 4, 2026, Sri Lanka was caught off-guard when the U.S. Navy submarine, the USS Charlotte, sank the Iranian frigate, IRIS Dena, 19 nautical miles off Sri Lanka’s southwest Galle coast. The attack left 104 crew members dead and brought the 2026 Iran war into subcontinental waters. The Sri Lanka Navy rescued thirty-two Iranian sailors, but the Sri Lankan government’s overall response drew criticism from opposition leaders.President Anura Kumara Dissanayake—head of the National People’s Power coalition, which is led by the Marxist-Leninist party, the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP)—clarified to the Sri Lankan parliament: “Our unwavering stance on this matter is one of neutrality.” But the opposition leader, Sajith Premadasa of the United National Party, challenged Dissanayake’s neutrality position as an excuse for passivity. The incident was “a death blow to Sri Lanka’s sovereignty,” Premadasa claimed as he pressed the president to condemn American and Israeli aggression against Iran as well as Iran’s targeting of other Gulf states. Former foreign minister G. L. Peiris was blunter: the “Sri Lankan government has actually insulted Iran, which is a friendly nation where Sri Lanka is concerned.” The opposition also questioned the government’s failure to act quickly on the Iranian frigate’s request to enter Sri Lankan territorial waters and its apparent lack of awareness of the USS Charlotte’s movements.Dissanayake’s foreign policy of neutrality offers Colombo room to focus on economic recovery, but, as the IRIS Dena incident shows, international economic and geopolitical turbulence will test how long that posture can be sustained. The country’s 2024 presidential elections offered much-needed political clarity after an acute economic crisis in 2022, the ouster of Sri Lanka’s president Gotabaya Rajapaksa amid the Aragalaya (Struggle) protests, and two years of political uncertainty. The NPP’s promise of reforms and the continuation of an International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout have been key to Sri Lanka’s post-2022 social contract.Yet with the current IMF loan cycle ending in 2027 and national elections due in 2029, early signs of volatility in Sri Lanka’s domestic and international politics are beginning to show. At home, the NPP’s inability to deliver many of its promised reforms signals that even if a 2022-style meltdown is unlikely, the economy remains under pressure. Unlike in 2022, however, a future crisis could strengthen a coercive left-wing one-party state rather than produce another popular uprising that sweeps a government from power. With regard to the country’s external relations, reliance on IMF funding—supported by an Indian backstop—has drawn Sri Lanka closer to India and the West. However, Chinese capital and finance, not just for infrastructure development but also through illicit networks, are also shaping Sri Lanka’s domestic and international politics. Looking to the future, Dissanayake’s principal challenge is to preserve the political and economic stability that his government has consolidated after 2024 while simultaneously managing multiple pressures that could unsettle both the NPP’s domestic moderation and its carefully calibrated foreign policy.Get more news and analysis fromCarnegie This WeekUnderstand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.Domestic Politics and the Limits of ReformSri Lanka turned a corner in September 2024 when the NPP coalition trounced traditional political parties and went on to win 159 of 225 parliamentary seats. The elections marked the start of a new political and economic journey for a country that had witnessed acute turmoil from 2022 to 2024. Dissanayake promised to use his electoral mandate to reform Sri Lanka’s economic and political structures to prevent a recurrence of a similar economic crisis. Yet beyond adhering to the IMF’s terms and conditions and tightening some anti-corruption regulations, much of the government’s broader reform agenda remains stalled. Three primary factors offer insight into the cause and consequences of this subpar performance: the risks associated with implementing reforms, tension between the JVP’s organizational nature and political character, and sensitive civil-military relations. A Stalled Reform Agenda In the run-up to the 2024 elections, Dissanayake promised to implement a series of reforms if the NPP was brought to power. These included combating corruption, reforming government institutions and the economy, improving living conditions, overhauling the taxation system, repealing the controversial Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) and the Online Safety Act, establishing independent prosecution and accountability mechanisms, and, most significantly, abolishing the executive presidency and its concentration of political power. These promises were made against the backdrop of a May 2023 IMF bailout that was negotiated by former president Ranil Wickremesinghe. Dissanayake agreed to continue with the loan agreement and meet its terms rather than seek to renegotiate it as the NPP had promised during the election campaign.Of these promised reforms, Colombo has made the greatest progress in complying with IMF requirements and pursuing modest anti-corruption measures. Thanks to the IMF program and political stability since 2024, the Sri Lankan economy surpassed expectations, recording a 5 percent growth in its GDP in 2024. Its foreign exchange reserves stood at $6.5 billion in June 2026 despite nearly a 10 percent decline in tourism due to the Iran war. This relative stability has persisted despite limited foreign investment, which stood at $1.04 billion in 2025, of which $352 million is in equity and $692 million is in the form of debt instruments. Anti-corruption measures—such as the Proceeds of Crime Act (2025) to recover assets, a stronger asset declaration system, mandatory reporting of audit-detected corruption, and proactive enforcement—have also helped fuel Sri Lanka’s overall economic rebound.But economic recovery and political consolidation have not led to delivery on other promised reforms. Though Dissanayake did abolish state-funded privileges for former presidents, he has failed to eliminate the executive presidency or repeal draconian security laws. In December 2025, Dissanayake’s Cabinet proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill to replace the PTA. (A supplementary gazette to this bill was presented in September 2026.) This bill is yet to pass the parliament, and it has kept intact several draconian PTA measures, such as prolonged pre-charge and pre-trial detention, as well as unchecked executive power to proscribe individuals and organizations without judicial oversight. Plans to overhaul the taxation system—admittedly a complex, technical, and time-consuming issue—and strengthen judicial independence remain confined within opaque committees with limited signs of visible progress. This raises the question of why a party with such a large mandate and economic stability has not moved more swiftly to deliver on its campaign promises.There are two compelling reasons for the slow pace of reforms. First, sequencing matters. Delaying certain economic measures allows Dissanayake to postpone the changes until the country formally meets IMF requirements. Additionally, as long as the economy remains stable, there is little public political pressure to initiate large-scale reforms. As the end of the current IMF program approaches in 2027, Colombo will focus its administrative energies on renegotiating the terms to secure more support. Against this backdrop, it makes little sense to launch sweeping taxation and judicial reforms while existential financial negotiations are ongoing. This is especially true if there is no clear political cost to be paid for inaction, given the dismal state of the opposition parties. The outcome of Dissanayake’s negotiations with the IMF, along with the JVP’s political standing in 2027–2028, will determine the government’s appetite for reform. The second reason the JVP has failed to push reforms is more politically straightforward. The existence of the executive presidency was a significant grievance for the JVP when it was the opposition, but the party enjoys the position’s outsized authority now that it holds the reins of power. Dissanayake is experiencing a rare moment wherein a Sinhala-dominated Marxist-Leninist party has come to power in Sri Lanka through the ballot box. The fact that it enjoys electoral support in the Tamil-dominated north and east as much as in the Sinhala-dominated south and central Sri Lanka is a testament to its appeal as an alternative to the traditional, family-based parties plagued by years of anti-incumbency. The JVP has little incentive to dilute the most powerful executive instrument to deliver on promises midway through its tenure, even if doing so was a core manifesto promise.The JVP: Marxist-Leninist Core, Social Democratic FaceThe NPP is a coalition of nearly twenty founding constituents that range from labor unions and collectives to the Sri Lanka Communist Party–Alternative Group. The JVP is the organizational and political core of this coalition, despite being a small cadre-based party with a history of anti-state militant activism during the 1970s and 1980s. It rose to power with an unexpectedly large mandate and knit together a coalition of multiple constituent parties, the latter of which has generated an underappreciated pressure to govern with caution and conservatism without rocking the proverbial boat. This caution has not only slowed reforms that could prove politically or socially disruptive, it has also begun to create a breach between the JVP’s organizational and ideological nature and its moderate political character.The JVP’s political pragmatism is fundamental to its national and international appeal. Dissanayake’s popularity, coupled with the JVP’s moderation on Sri Lanka’s religious and ethnic fault lines, affords the party a social democratic demeanor that is less strident than its Marxist-Leninist underpinnings. For Jayadeva Uyangoda, a senior political scientist and former JVP leader, such a shift is more than tactical: “It was a decision taken by the politburo, and the JVP has transformed itself into a social democratic party.”1Yet the way the Dissanayake government operates reveals a different side of the party. Almost all government decisions are taken by the JVP’s politburo, not by the president’s office alone. “There is no difference between the party and the government,” Uyangoda says.2 Led by party General Secretary Tilvin Silva, the six-member politburo includes Dissanayake (leader), Vijitha Herath (information secretary), K.D. Lalkantha (administrative secretary), Bimal Rathnayake (national organizer), and Sunil Handunneththi (financial secretary). Lalkantha, who is also a cabinet minister of agriculture, livestock, lands, and irrigation, recently claimed that “we have the government’s power, but we must continue our struggle to capture state power. Only then will our struggle be complete, in a way.”The Marxist-Leninist nature of the JVP works against its social democratic character, and the tension that this creates is beginning to surface. Many members of the NPP who do not belong to the JVP are either joining the party to feel like an “insider” or the “real deal” or are becoming disillusioned with the JVP’s dominance. Some fear that Dissanayake, the popular president, has ceded too much authority to the more senior party figure Tilvin Silva, creating a parallel power center that is more assertive and committed to Leninism than to social democracy. Arguably, if the politburo is the principal decisionmaking body, then the general secretary could be perceived as being more powerful within the party’s hierarchy and method of operations than Dissanayake, the designated party leader.Inspired by the “democratic” characteristics of China’s political system, Silva publicly stated last year that the NPP needs to be “in power for 15, 20 or 25 years . . . to [be able to] take the country forward under one vision, one policy framework.” He was quick to emphasize JVP’s continued embrace of electoral politics, but his remarks, his participation in government decisionmaking, and JVP’s inaction to abolish the executive presidency have collectively raised concerns about JVP’s ambition to turn Sri Lanka into a one-party state. “These are the early signs of what is to come . . . the JVP will show its true ideological colours in its second term when it is more experienced and more secure in power,” says Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu, founder and executive director of the Centre for Policy Alternatives.3This debate between an elected presidency and a politburo of a Marxist-Leninist party helps explain why Dissanayake is incentivized to keep the executive presidency intact. In addition to diluting an executive instrument that is helping Dissanayake deliver a modicum of prosperity, the presidency also helps him balance Silva’s power in the politburo. Dissanayake’s popularity and moderation are powerful assets for the JVP and could give him leverage in the event of an internal party split if the situation deteriorates. The JVP has experienced several splits in the past, including the 2008 Sinhala-nationalist breakaway faction of ten parliamentarians who created the National Freedom Front and the 2011–2012 split of ultra-Marxists who formed the Frontline Socialist Party.In 2015, when Dissanayake succeeded Somawansa Amarasinghe as party leader, the latter left the JVP to create a separate political outfit. To put this in perspective, Silva has been party secretary since 1995. Known as “Tilvin Ayya” (elder brother), Silva has considerable hold over the JVP’s rank and file, but it is unclear how he will use his influence to steer the government and what pressures it might create within the party. Regardless of the opacity surrounding his precise role, the JVP politburo’s emergence as a parallel power center is raising concerns among observers. From renegotiating the IMF loan and abolishing the executive presidency to changing the tax laws and enabling judicial independence, the JVP politburo’s concept of power and how to exercise it remains at odds with the Dissanayake government’s social democratic character. If, for instance, Sri Lanka enters another crisis cycle—likely if structural reforms beyond the IMF’s short-term remedies are not implemented—the NPP’s reaction to public protests could prove truer to the party’s original, coercive, Marxist-Leninist charter than to its more recent embrace of social democracy.Civil-Military Relations and the Tamil QuestionCivil-military relations remain sensitive in Sri Lanka’s post-2022 social contract. Though civilian control over the military makes it unambiguous that the president holds the defense portfolio, the NPP has been reluctant to directly challenge the military. The most important fault line concerns accountability for human rights violations during the 2009 civil war. Since the last general election, there has been little movement on this issue from the Sri Lankan government. The October 2025 Resolution 60/1 of the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) underscores the need to hold those who committed human rights violations and carried out extrajudicial killings to account. The NPP government has been cautious not to push this cause too strongly for fear of upsetting a fragile civil-military equilibrium. Dissanayake has pressed the army to return private land to Tamil citizens in the north and east but has achieved only limited success.The civil-military balance in Sri Lanka is tied not just to wartime abuses and their aftermath, but also the issue of political autonomy for Sri Lankan Tamils and the devolution of policing and land powers. The Thirteenth Amendment to the Sri Lankan constitution, adopted in November 1987 under Indian pressure and a raging Tamil insurgency, is a constitutional reform that promised devolution of powers, created nine provincial councils, and devolved certain powers such as education, health, agriculture, housing, local government, and roads from the center to the provinces. Crucially, it also recognized Tamil as an official language alongside Sinhala and established English as a link language. Yet the amendment has still not been fully implemented.In 2024, the NPP’s election manifesto promised a new constitution that incorporates devolution and equality for Sri Lanka’s Tamil communities. Dissanayake reaffirmed that commitment in August 2026 to Tamil and Muslim political parties. But the details of the promised new constitution, the specific nature of devolution, and the timing of provincial council elections are not forthcoming. Of all the provisions contained in the Thirteenth Amendment, only some have been implemented. Tamil is now recognized as an official language, and English as a link language. But access to Tamil translation for the police, courts, and government administration remains uneven. Provincial councils exist on paper, but they have been dormant for nearly a decade. The central government retains command over policing, land, and finance, even though ordinary public services such as schools, roads, hospitals, and housing have seen increased local leadership. Such partial implementation of the amendment helps preserve the power of armed forces in Tamil areas, weakens elected civilian institutions in the northern and eastern provinces, and keeps Sri Lanka’s civil-military balance in favor of civilian leadership in Colombo. The NPP has nevertheless initiated greater scrutiny of security agencies by following through on the prosecution of security officials tied to the previous government. The arrest of former military-intelligence and State Intelligence Service chief, Major General (Retd.) Suresh Sallay for allegedly aiding and abetting the 2019 Easter Sunday suicide bombers that left 270 people dead including forty-five children serves as a case in point. Separate to the Sallay investigation, Sri Lanka’s High Court recently convicted fifteen men over the bombings. The attacks created a climate of fear that helped Rajapaksa win the 2019 presidential elections on the platform centered on national security. Sallay is said to be aligned with the Rajapaksa family and allegedly helped mastermind the attack in order to mobilize public support for Rajapaksa. From the NPP’s perspective, the arrest of Sallay among other accused has helped the government reinforce its credibility and deliver on the promise of accountability.Foreign Policy and the Limits of NeutralityConversations in Colombo about foreign policy are relaxed, a reflection of the government’s attitude that “foreign policy is not a priority issue,” as argued by Saravanamuttu.4 The IRIS Dena incident was an acute but temporary test of Dissanayake’s determination to steer clear of great-power rivalry in and around Sri Lanka. For now, Colombo’s neutrality is bearing fruit, and it suits regional and extra-regional powers such as India and China. But as Sri Lanka’s domestic politics evolve and geopolitical fault lines harden, that equilibrium could prove difficult to sustain. Sri Lankan foreign policy has swung before: The Rajapaksa government tilted in China’s direction in the 2010s, while the National Unity Alliance government led by Maithripala Sirisena moved closer to India and the West.Today, Sri Lanka’s commitment to neutrality is driven by its economic circumstances and a post-2022 tacit geopolitical balancing act with three external powers. This balancing act consists of rebuilding strategic trust with India, managing China’s financial and strategic footprint, and containing Western pressure on human rights. Colombo adopted this strategy in response to the sobering reality that none of these powers immediately came to Sri Lanka’s rescue during the 2022 crisis. China’s refusal to alter the terms of its loans as Sri Lanka approached financial collapse contrasted with India’s eventual provision of $4 billion offer in relief, and the experience has had a profound impact on the Sri Lankan elite’s foreign policy beliefs and calculations. “There is a clear understanding in the society here that India will not let Sri Lanka go under,” Saravanamuttu adds.5 This is why the NPP, despite being traditionally anti-India and ideologically aligned with the Communist Party of China, built such strong ties with India. However, this foreign policy equilibrium could be disrupted if Sri Lanka faces renewed international pressure on human rights violations, another economic crisis, or major power military hostilities in the Indian Ocean vicinity.Human Rights and Geopolitical LeverageFrom Colombo’s perspective, the current equilibrium is both desirable and sustainable. But this could change if Colombo again faces pressure on its human rights record the way it has in the past. In the late 2000s and early 2010s, president Mahinda Rajapaksa’s decision to tilt in favor of China was, in part, driven by sustained Western and Indian pressure on human rights and also demands for accountability at the United Nations. As of today, neither Sri Lanka nor human rights are a priority of the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump. Sergio Gor, U.S. special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, visited Sri Lanka in March 2026 to discuss trade and investment with Dissanayake, but he did not raise the issue of human rights. This relative disengagement contrasts sharply with Washington’s historic activist posture, including its diplomatic pressure on Colombo during Sri Lanka’s civil war and its coordination with India as a way of countering the Chinese footprint during the 2010s.The erosion of liberal norms in the West and the UN’s reduced credibility means that Colombo faces far less external pressure to prioritize human rights than it once did. Even though European countries continue to press Colombo to account for excesses, this issue has lost some of its strategic significance. The UNHRC’s Resolution 60/1 underscores Colombo’s lack of action but does not hold sufficient political weight to alter the government’s behavior. For its part, China has never raised this issue at all. Beijing’s silence on what it views as Sri Lanka’s internal affairs helped China build political and strategic capital in Colombo during the Rajapaksa years, culminating in a ninety-nine-year lease on the Hambantota port in 2017.The only country that can seriously pressure Sri Lanka on the human rights issue is India. During the Rajapaksa years, New Delhi felt that Colombo was deliberately countering India by inviting Chinese investments. Colombo’s decision to allow the docking of a Chinese naval submarine and warship at the port of Colombo in 2014 was seen as crossing a red line for India’s security-strategic interests. During this period, India not only coordinated with the United States to pile pressure on Colombo at the UN over its dismal human rights record, but it also pressured Sri Lanka to fully implement the Thirteenth Amendment in coordination with Sri Lankan Tamil parties.The Dissanayake government’s promise of holding provincial council elections is in keeping with the amendment, but full implementation remains a sensitive matter. The Thirteenth Amendment created provincial councils as a form of power sharing, but no provincial elections have been held since 2014. This has resulted in the governor, a presidential appointee, making decisions, thereby further undermining the idea of devolution of power. “NPP does not want New Delhi to be seen as the benefactor of Sri Lankan Tamils. It wants to take the political credit for holding the long-delayed provincial council elections as well as a new package of devolution, framed independent of the Indo-Lanka Accord and 13th amendment,” says Uyangoda.6 The combination of the amendment and human rights accountability offers India considerable leverage over Colombo. How New Delhi exercises such leverage is a political choice. In August 2026, Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited Colombo and “called upon the Sri Lankan leadership to implement their commitment to hold Provincial Council elections at the earliest and to fully implement the Constitutional provisions of Sri Lanka to meet the aspirations of the Tamil people.” But Misri did not mention the Thirteenth Amendment directly and stopped short of imposing a timeline on when elections must occur. From India’s perspective, using this issue to exercise leverage risks undermining the strategic trust that has emerged between the two neighbors.ArticleSri Lanka’s Elusive Democratic RenewalOne year after a historic election, Sri Lanka’s new left-leaning government faces mounting pressure to translate its reform promises into action.China and India: Competing Economic and Strategic FootprintsAnother economic crisis or future military confrontation in the Indian Ocean between India and China or the United States and China could also disrupt Sri Lanka’s fragile balancing act Sri Lanka’s inability to overhaul its economic fundamentals is the biggest risk factor that could lead to another crash. Colombo needs to find ways to generate revenue that go beyond tourism, agriculture, and international remittances. Other than pushing Colombo to negotiate another IMF bailout, the next crisis would also raise the stakes for both Beijing and New Delhi, as they will be forced to rethink their overseas developmental strategies in Sri Lanka. As of now, China’s developmental footprint is more capital-intensive and concentrated in large physical assets, whereas India’s $7.5 billion worth of total assistance is more geographically dispersed and people-centered.In addition to the construction and operation of the Hambantota port and the Colombo port city built on reclaimed land, China has also invested in the Colombo International Container Terminal. It built several expressways, financed and constructed the Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport, developed the Norochcholai/Lakvijaya coal power plant, and contributed to other smaller development projects. Most of these projects are in southern, Sinhala-dominated regions. In contrast, India’s projects have had a stronger imprint in the north: the reconstruction and upgrading of the Northern Railway; financing of smaller road and bridge projects in the north and east; funding support for the Palaly/Jaffna International Airport; developing the Sampur Solar project; financing the Indian Housing Project in northern, eastern, and plantation regions; and supporting other smaller projects. India is also helping with the refurbishment of the Kankesanthurai port in the north, developing the Colombo West International Terminal, and planning to develop the port city Trincomalee as an energy, industrial, and logistical hub.Arguably, India’s people-centric strategy has generated more political dividends than China’s capital-intensive engagement. Beijing’s investments have not created much goodwill in Sri Lanka. Silva’s ideological and political admiration for China is not widely shared across Sri Lankan society, emphasizing the limited popular appeal of the JVP’s ideological orientation and the party’s reliance on Dissanayake’s mass appeal. In fact, an apparent increase in Chinese organized-crime activity, including a recent mafia-linked murder in Colombo, and Beijing’s decision to forgo support for Colombo in 2022 has further reduced China’s geopolitical appeal in Sri Lanka. To correct these perceptions, Beijing recently shared intelligence on several Chinese mafia syndicates operating in Sri Lanka and requested Colombo to crack down on such activities. Unless China steps in during a future crisis to support Sri Lanka as India did in 2022, it is unlikely to regain a foothold on the island the way India has. The two countries’ response to Cyclone Ditwah in 2026 is instructive: India offered Colombo a relief package of $450 million, including $100 million in grants and the remainder provided through concessional credit lines. By contrast, China only offered $1 million in emergency cash assistance coupled with disaster relief worth RMB 1 million (approx. $148,959) through the party-to-party channel. The Red Cross Society of China topped this with another $100,000 in special aid funds. Given these shifting realities, another economic crisis would likely push Colombo further toward India, not China.Lastly, as the sinking of IRIS Dena demonstrated, there is certainly a chance of military hostilities between major powers in the Indian Ocean in the coming years. If such a naval clash occurs, it could significantly dislocate Colombo’s triple lock. Any kinetic conflict between China and India or the United States and China in or near Sri Lankan waters would make it far harder for Colombo to avoid choosing sides. Colombo avoided such a trade-off during the 2026 Iran war when it refused an Iranian request to host three Iranian naval vessels for a goodwill visit and rejected an American request to land two fighter jets at the Mattala airport. However, if the combatants in a future conflict include either China or India, Colombo’s adherence to neutrality will be difficult to sustain.In this respect, the 2025 India-Sri Lanka defense memorandum of understanding and the visit of Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh to Colombo in September, the first of its kind in nearly four decades, offers clues. While falling far short of establishing a military alliance, the agreement signals Sri Lanka’s general tilt in favor of India and the West on the security-strategic affairs of the Indian Ocean Region (IOR). Colombo has effectively and indefinitely paused visits by Chinese research vessels, or “spy ships,” to Sri Lankan ports. In March 2026, it refused the request of Chinese research vessel Shi Yan 6 to enter its territorial waters. Such caution on sensitive security-strategic issues demonstrates Colombo’s carefully calibrated balancing act vis-à-vis China, which remains an important economic partner.Conclusion: A Fragile Balance Sri Lanka has come a long way from the 2022 Aragalaya protests. Its economy is showing signs of revival, and its polity is stable under the leadership of Dissanayake. The IMF loan, coupled with financial support from India, has helped Sri Lanka weather a troubled economic patch. The sinking of the IRIS Dena by the U.S. Navy in March tested Sri Lanka’s foreign policy principles, but Colombo maintained a neutral posture without provoking either Iran or the United States. The duration of this phase of stability will depend on whether the NPP’s failure to deliver promised structural reforms triggers another economic crisis in the coming years and on the direction of negotiations with the IMF in 2027. The tension between the JVP’s Marxist-Leninist nature and social democratic character could also play out differently if the economy comes under greater strain. The government’s current moderation on ethnic and social fault lines could pave the way for a more coercive Marxist-Leninist style of governance.On the foreign policy front, Sri Lanka’s neutrality rests on a balancing act with its three principal external partners: India, China, and the United States. If relations between these three powers deteriorate to the point of military hostilities in the IOR, the equilibrium could collapse and push Sri Lanka to pick sides. But, absent such a confrontation, Sri Lanka is likely to maintain its position of engaging with China economically while limiting Beijing’s strategic footprint on the island. In contrast, it will widen and deepen relations with India on both economic and strategic fronts. India, for its part, is likely to continue supporting Colombo, even if it fails to implement the Thirteenth Amendment fully in Tamil areas, provided Sri Lanka does not allow China to use its territory and ports to undermine India’s security-strategic interests. That strategic logic may endure even if the JVP takes a more coercive, one-party turn. French government bonds, or OATs, are under growing pressure. While rising yields reflect a broader sell-off across European markets, concerns over France’s fiscal trajectory and political uncertainty are driving an additional risk premium.
In this episode of Barclays Brief, host Patrick Coffey is joined by Rohan Khanna, Head of European Rates Strategy, to examine why investors are demanding greater clarity before returning to French debt. They consider how persistent budget deficits, substantial debt issuance and political fragmentation have contributed to the widening OAT-Bund spread, and why the 2027 presidential and parliamentary elections will be critical for market confidence.
Khanna also draws an important distinction for investors: the pressure on French bonds reflects a repricing of France’s fiscal and political risk, not a repeat of the 2011–12 eurozone debt crisis. Looking ahead, attention will turn to whether the next administration will have the willingness and ability to address France’s fiscal trajectory. Until there is greater clarity, volatility may persist and investors could continue to demand a higher risk premium for holding French debt.
Clients can read more on Barclays Live:

French banks: Standing OAT of the crowd
Euro Area: Rates Strategy - OAT of the frying pan into the fire
Macro x Politics: Not just another French election
Thinking Macro: Three stories. Not one.

Listeners can also explore the topic further:

US Rates: Higher for longer
Decoding the bond sell-off
European rates: Inflation & AI waves collide

Important Content Disclosures

Transcript

Patrick
I'm Patrick Coffey. This is the Barclays brief. And today we're focused on France. And that's because there have been some very big moves in the French government bond market, as investors grapple with the country's fiscal outlook and the rose to the 2027 French election. Quick bit of jargon busting before we get into it. So today you're going to hear us talk about the OAT or the OAT Bund spread. OATs are French government bonds and Bunds are German government bonds. So, the spread is simply the gap between their borrowing costs. And it's a useful gauge of how investors are viewing the risk around French debt compared with German debt. And it also gives our research analysts a great opportunity to put a pun in the title of their notes. So, this week we've had OAT of control, OATs gone wild, and my favourite OAT of the frying pan into the fire. Now the author of that note is Rohan Khanna, our European Rates Analyst. Rohan, thanks a lot for joining.
Rohan
Thanks, Patrick. Great to be here. And in fact, this is perfect timing because I am here in Paris at our inaugural European Macro Conference. And this is exactly what everyone wants to talk about.
Patrick
Indeed, indeed. So European bond yields have been rising sharply. Of course the US has as well. But investors right now seem particularly focused on France. What's driving that concern?
Rohan
To be fair, France has been in the markets crosshairs since President Macron called a snap election in June 2024. It left the parliament in a very fragmented state, and France now has its fifth Prime Minister in the last three years. Now, this rise in political uncertainty came at a time when France's fiscal fundamentals were already weakening for a considerable amount of time. Precisely because of this reason, budget negotiations in 2024, 2025 have been periods of significant market stress. For 2026, this has been a perfect storm for European bonds and specifically for French debt. That's because the Gulf conflict put the ECB on a rate hike path, and all the calm that the market had observed over the last year went away. On top of that, France has to issue a lot of debt. But once again, it's come down to the budget. Now France is presenting its 2027 budget. They've had to once again increase the deficit estimate for 2026. They were targeting for -5%. It's expected to be -5.4. And they've set an ambitious target for next year at -5%.
Patrick
Indeed. And when the budget was announced a couple of weeks ago, there was a bit of scepticism, to say the least, about some of those forecasts for 2027. And now everyone's very focused on the French election, which isn't until April next year. How much does the outcome of that election matter for markets, and what are the polls telling us today?
Rohan
Absolutely. I mean, the polls matter immensely, given the market wants to see willingness and ability from policymakers to address France's domestic challenges. Now, you mentioned that there was some scepticism about the budget forecasts. And that's absolutely right. Our economists, the High Council of Public Finances in France, which is the budget watchdog, both believe that the government's growth forecasts for next year are quite optimistic. So the market wants to see a credible political solution for France's growth and fiscal challenges. And this is where the parliamentary elections and the presidential elections become so important. Now if you look at opinion polls, they are pointing to one of the largest and most significant political resets in France's history. If you look at the first-round opinion polls, they are pointing to Madame Le Pen having a clean victory. And in the second round, most opinion polls again suggest that Madame Le Pen is likely going to be the winner. But the story doesn't end with the presidential election, because whoever wins is very likely to call a parliamentary election, and it will be the shape of the parliament in terms of whether there is any party that can get an absolute majority. Or will we once again have the muddle through minority government that has been in place since Mr. Macron’s second presidency. That is what the market wants to see, because if we are stuck in the same situation as we are today where we have a minority government, then getting anything done is going to be very difficult. So, your challenges of high deficits, ever increasing debt to GDP are going to get even harder to be addressed if there is not an absolute majority to address those difficult challenges.
Patrick
Okay, so put it together. We've got scepticism at the current budget, and we've got a lot of uncertainty around the winner of the French election. Let's then talk about bonds, which is your area of absolute expertise. And think about the OAT Bund spread. How much of the move in that spread do you think reflects the broader bond market dynamics that we talked about here on the Barclays Brief a lot. And how much is specifically about French politics and French public finances.
Rohan
If we reflect on what's happened with OAT Bunds since June, and I'm going to kind of benchmark it to June, because that's where things blew up really. OAT Bunds would have widened between 60 to 70 basis points. Now remember bond yields have risen everywhere. Ten-year German yields have risen by about 60 to 70 basis points. Ten-year OAT yields of French yields have risen by about 120 to 130 basis points. And across the EGB complex you've seen yields go up. So it's not just a France story, but the widening that you see in OAT Bunds is a reflection of the idiosyncratic French specific dynamics where you have deficits, you have a budget that has to be decided and on top of that, you have political uncertainty. Now, if you reflect on what is the market telling you, the markets telling you that the level of uncertainty and the challenges that the French policymakers face are causing a buyer strike. Market participants want more clarity and credibility before they can go back and buy OATs at these level of spreads, but the runway between now and the election is quite long, so we are probably stuck in a period of prolonged uncertainty.
Patrick
Yeah. You described it at the start here as a perfect storm in France. Do you think the bond market has now priced in all of this bad news, or is the market still waking up to the fiscal risks in France?
Rohan
If we look at a very long chart, Patrick, what we'll see is that the current level of ten-year France versus German spread or the OAT Bund spread is higher than any time since the European debt crisis of 2011, 2012. But this is where it's important to keep things in perspective, because the political reset and the fiscal math that France faces are both so challenging that, in our opinion, the spread is unbounded. We need to work through the wall of worry and the fog of uncertainty before we can confidently say that the market is pricing the right thing for OATs. So in our view, the market is waking up to the fiscal risks. The political uncertainty is a big deterrent for buyers to step in. And we may have not seen the worst.
Patrick
Okay. So we may not have seen the worst. I imagine that some of our listeners will immediately think back to the eurozone crisis. How valid is that comparison? And is this primarily a French story or could it be something bigger?
Rohan
That's a great question, Patrick. And absolutely, the way bond markets have behaved over the last month, it is indeed reminiscent of the behaviour during the European debt crisis. But I think we should draw a clear difference between that episode, which was a case of everything everywhere all at once, versus this episode, which is an idiosyncratic, France specific issue from a banking sector perspective. I don't think the kind of sovereign bank nexus that was prevalent back in the debt crisis is really applicable. But most importantly, this is about fiscal trajectories. France’s fiscal trajectory is clearly upward sloping, meaning debt to GDP is set to rise under various circumstances. When you look at Spain, Portugal, Greece, these are clearly examples of countries where debt to GDP is a downward sloping trajectory. So it is drawing a comparison with European debt crisis I think is incorrect at this instance because this is clearly a crisis where fiscal trajectories are divergent and the market is waking up to what France’s fiscal trajectory really holds.
Patrick
Okay, that's definitely a relief. But now let's think about the road to the 2027 French election. What are the key milestones and the risks that investors should be watching right now?
Rohan
I think people are going to be very focused on the evolution of opinion polls, because if there is a situation where the second round becomes a tussle between Madame Le Pen and Mr. Mélenchon, then you have two far right and far left candidates going up against each other, and that is potentially a negative outcome for the market.
Patrick
Okay. And so last thing. We're recording this on Wednesday the 7th of October. And just yesterday Madame Le Pen held a press conference introducing their economic manifesto she's going to put forward as their and I quote, “counter budget for 2027”. Just very briefly, what's the market reaction to that press conference yesterday?
Rohan
In spirit, we can draw comfort from the fact that she's making the right noises. She understands that France is having a significant challenge on the fiscal front, and that needs to be addressed. Otherwise, the markets are going to have an even severe tantrum. So in spirit, you have to give full marks. The problem, though, is implementation. And this is the frustrating bit because having seen this widening, even the most ardent believers in the France story who want to be long OATs have to still wait to see the outcome of the election, to see who becomes prime minister, who becomes finance minister, and whether the new administration, in whatever shape or form it takes, has the willingness and the ability to implement the proposals that have been laid out.
Patrick
So the road ahead is long in France. Rohan, thanks so much for joining me today. This has been fascinating and great to hear from you.
Rohan
Thank you Patrick.
Patrick
Now there's likely to be more volatility ahead, and markets may yet demand a higher risk premium for French debt. But for all the concern, Rohan has made it clear that this is not 2011 and the eurozone crisis. The story today is a repricing of French fiscal and political risk, not an existential threat to the euro area. If you've enjoyed today's episode with Rohan, do hit subscribe and will be back next week with more from The Barclays Brief.

About the experts

Rohan Khanna

Head of European Rates Strategy

Rohan Khanna is a Managing Director and Head of European Rates Strategy. Based in London, Rohan is responsible for interest rates research across cash, derivative and money markets in Europe. Prior to joining Barclays in June 2023, he held similar position at UBS AG and prior to that was a rates strategist at Goldman Sachs. He has also worked as a FX trader and a visiting faculty in previous roles. Rohan holds a MSc in Economics from London School of Economics and a Bachelor in Engineering and MBA Finance specialisations from India.

Patrick Coffey

Global Head of the Product Management Group at Research

Patrick Coffey is a Managing Director and Global Head of the Product Management Team in Research. Previously, he was Deputy Head of European Equity Research and prior to this, he was an equity research analyst for a decade. Patrick was consistently a Top 3 ranked analyst within the No. 1 ranked leisure team (Extel survey 2014-19). Before joining Barclays in 2013, Patrick worked for four years at Liberum as a Leisure analyst and has also held roles at Manchester United and in strategy consulting. Patrick received a Master’s from Oxford University in History of Art and has a First Class joint honours degree from Nottingham University in History of Art and English Literature and Language.

articles.title: Markets weigh rising yields and AI exuberance
articles.text:
Investment Talks

Macroeconomics

Equity

Fixed income

Volatility

Diversification

7 October, 2026

10 minutes

Markets weigh rising yields and AI exuberance

EDM

Investment TalksENFR

Markets weigh rising yields and AI exuberance

10 minutes

EDM

Investment TalksENFR

Summary

Bond volatility has become the main feature of recent market moves. Equities have remained relatively resilient, but bond yields have moved higher in a context in which markets are becoming more sensitive to macro data and policy expectations. As yields move higher and news flows evolve, markets are readjusting across countries and curves. Global bond markets have been the first to readjust, but we have recently seen moves in global credit markets too.The moves are being driven by several overlapping forces. Tensions in the Middle East have kept oil prices elevated and added to inflation pressure, while stronger US activity data in recent weeks and heavy corporate issuance linked to the AI build-out have pushed long-term yields higher. While benefiting from solid fundamentals, European bonds are under pressure from risks related to energy prices and inflation, reinforced by some fiscal and political concerns, including in France.For investors, the key implication is the need for a more active approach in fixed income and stronger diversification. Higher yields are improving the appeal of bonds, which now offer yields not seen in decades, but as flows adjust across countries and segments, we see volatility remaining high and dispersion rising in the credit space. In this environment, an active and globally diversified approach to fixed income remains important, with a preference for higher-quality bonds. At the same time, while equities are well supported by strong earnings, prospects for higher inflation and higher yields will increase scrutiny on balance sheets, and on excess capital and debt build-out in the AI ecosystem. This will call for more selection and increase diversification at sector level and across asset classes.

What has been happening recently in global financial markets?

Market volatility has increased in recent weeks, particularly in bond markets. The MOVE index, a measure of expected volatility in US Treasuries, has been rising significantly, decoupling from the VIX equity volatility indicator in an unusual move. This is significantly different from the March volatility spike that affected both markets at the start of the Iran war. While equities have remained resilient and continue to be dominated by the AI capex story, bond yields have been rising sharply over recent weeks. The US 10-year Treasury yield was around 4.7% in late August, moved above 5% for the first time since 2023 on 15 September, and briefly touched 5.34% on 1 October, its highest level since 2002, before easing back into the weekend. Major equity markets also saw more marked swings but closed the past week with overall little change (-0.3% for the S&P 500, -1.1% for the STOXX Europe 600).

What are the reasons behind this volatility?

We are seeing a rotation, particularly within bond markets, as investors exit areas of higher perceived risk to reduce overall portfolio volatility.

Different forces are driving markets, and their interaction is what makes the environment particularly complex.Middle East tensions and the oil outlook. Escalating tensions in the Middle East over the summer, and the lack of clarity around when the war may end, have kept energy markets highly volatile. In recent days, demand concerns and some easing of the most acute fears have pulled prices back, but Brent remains in the $95 to $110 range, well above the $87 average seen between June and August. This weighs especially on European bonds, as Europe is more exposed to rising oil and gas prices. The G7 leaders’ decision last week to release up to 100 million barrels from emergency oil and diesel reserves to ease pressure on energy prices may help to further stabilise markets.Growth, inflation and the Federal Reserve. Long-term yields have moved higher on the back of stronger signals on US economic activity, rising inflation risks stemming from the war and heightened competition for capital from heavy corporate issuance to finance the AI build-out. That is happening against a backdrop of positive earnings results and supportive market sentiment, which has helped risk assets remain resilient, but it has also led investors to demand more compensation for bonds.France and European bond volatility. Rising political uncertainty around the French budget, at a time of increasing debt levels, broader global spillover from higher bond yields and upcoming elections next year, has added another source of volatility in European bonds.As a result, we are seeing a rotation, particularly within bond markets, as investors try to reduce overall portfolio volatility. This is visible in global credit, where corporate bond spreads have recently started to widen. Here, record AI capex and debt issuance have also been a major driver with rising market scrutiny. In European government bonds, we have seen further spread widening in French bonds with spillovers into Italian and other peripheral bonds, and a “flight to safety” into German Bunds. These are, in our view, orderly rotations that are part of the re-adjustment to a backdrop of higher rates and higher inflation risks.

What is happening in France?

Uncertainty until next year’s elections is likely to drive persistent volatility in French bonds, but the recent spread widening may have gone too far.

This week also saw France present its budget on 1 October. The government proposed a €54 billion fiscal consolidation effort, targeting a public deficit of 5.0% of GDP in 2027. Under the proposed budget, the adjustment starts from a position where the government expects the 2026 deficit to reach 5.4% of GDP, compared with the 5.0% target set only a few months ago. On the same day, France’s independent public finance council — the Haut Conseil des Finances Publiques (HCFP) — issued a formal assessment describing the government’s economic assumptions as optimistic.We believe the most likely scenario is one of gradual consolidation, which would not fully resolve the medium-term fiscal challenge. The market has already become more watchful on French government debt in recent weeks, given the approaching budget deadline, higher debt-servicing costs and political uncertainty ahead of next year’s elections. Current market pricing reflects this uncertainty, as shown by the widening spread between France’s ten-year government bond yield and Bunds. However, it remains below previous crisis levels, and we see this move driven more by foreign investor outflows than by genuine concerns France enters this phase of uncertainty from a position of relative strength, helped by a decade of exceptionally low rates and an overall high-quality sovereign profile. This has helped France keep the average maturity of its debt at around 8–9 years, which limits the risk of a refinancing wall and immediate exposure to rising interest rates. France also benefits from a large and diversified economy, with a strategic position in Europe. It is well placed in many export areas, including luxury goods and defence. Demographic ageing is also less of a challenge than elsewhere in Europe, while higher labour productivity, strong household savings and relatively low electricity prices can help the French economy remain resilient in the current geopolitical context.This has led over time to an increased share of foreign investor ownership in French debt, at around 56%, reflecting strong demand, but also leaving the market more exposed as higher global yields offer investors better opportunities elsewhere. Until next year’s elections, volatility in French bonds is likely to persist as investors reassess the medium-term fiscal trajectory and adjust to higher yields globally. That said, we may already have seen the worst of the adjustment.

What are the main implications for investors?

Bond yields are increasingly attractive, but volatility is likely to stay high, calling for an active approach to bond investing.

Bond markets are being shaken by unusual volatility. This reflects a regime shift towards a world shaped by geopolitical ruptures, inflationary pressures driven by demand for investment in AI, the climate transition, and increasing debt. At the same time, recent rises in bond yields are making bonds increasingly attractive to investors, with yields now at levels not seen in decades. In this environment, an active and globally diversified approach to bonds is key. In credit we expect dispersion to rise, as the market reassess the impact of higher rates across different sectors and businesses. Here we maintain a preference for high-quality bonds less exposed to the challenge of rising rates.

articles.title: The Chip War Comes To Southeast Asia
articles.text:
The Chip War Comes To Southeast Asia

Tom Miller

Gavekal Research | 8 Oct 2026

In July, the White House fired a warning shot in the artificial-intelligence arms race with China. It accused Chinese startup Moonshot AI of training its models using Nvidia’s most advanced chips, hosted in data centers in Thailand. This legal workaround enabled Moonshot to bypass strict US controls on chip exports to China.Washington is now moving to close the loophole that allows Chinese AI labs to rent access to restricted chips in third countries. The loophole is global, but Southeast Asia is the most important battleground because of its huge data-center buildout and economic ties to both powers. A crackdown could take some of the heat out of the region’s multi-billion-dollar digital investment boom, damaging an important driver of growth. It is the latest in a series of challenges to Southeast Asia’s long-held policy of hedging between the superpowers (see Southeast Asia Plays Both Sides In The US-China Rivalry). Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia all want to be neutral digital hubs. Washington wants them to pick sides.

Welcome back to Market Matters, October edition.
It been about 2 months since we had the US Treasury/Bessent announcement with respect long end bond liquidity support, which begin September 9th. Since then, yields have continued marching higher, with the 10Y surging through 5% to levels last seen in 2007. This was compounded by the Fed’s decision to increase the target rate by 25bps at the last FOMC meeting.
The Iran War continues to be a thorn in the side of markets, specifically oil. Oil prices have resumed their upward trajectory, continuing to put pressure on governments and markets alike.
Gold has sold off and given up most of it’s gains from the last few months.
Equities remain resilient and continue grinding towards all time highs, even as breadth continues to narrow.
Crypto markets have shown a patch of relative strength with BTC almost pushing into the $90K region. We have also seen a resurgence in overall risk appetite among crypto participants since the August US Treasury announcement. Over the last few weeks, however, crypto markets and risk appetite appear to be waning.
In this month’s episode, we highlight our updated Delphi Unified Macro Regime Model, which no incorporates drivers of liquidity, growth, and inflation while taking into account positioning. We lay out the backdrop as we move into year end. We then dive deeper into crypto markets to look under the hood and discuss crypto’s recent weakness and what it means going forward.
Are we back? Is there still room to run? Or is the party ending? You wont want to miss this month’s episode.
